transcript.text: We replaced our old condenser dryer with a heat pump one about a month ago and honestly it's driving me mad, a normal load of towels takes nearly 3 and a half hours, the old one did it in about 90 minutes. It also feels barely warm for the first half hour when I open the door to check. Surely that's not right? Is it faulty?

Before you start, switch it off and unplug it. It is very likely that your dryer is working correctly. A heat-pump tumble dryer operates on a refrigeration cycle (like a fridge running in reverse), which means it dries at a much lower temperature than an old condenser or vented dryer. It is completely normal for the air to feel only 'barely warm' and for a load of towels to take significantly longer—often 2.5 to 3 hours—to dry thoroughly. The fact that it feels cool in the first half hour is also typical, as the machine spends time heating up its internal components before drying effectively. 1. Clean the filters: Remove and rinse both the lint filter (in the door) and the condenser/evaporator unit (usually behind a panel at the bottom front). If these are clogged with fluff, airflow is restricted and drying times increase dramatically.
2. Check the load size and wetness: Ensure you aren't overloading the drum (it should be no more than two-thirds full) that the towels were spun well in the washing machine before being transferred. If the filters are clean and the load was normal, please let me know if the clothes come out damp at the end of a cycle. If they come out dry but just take longer, it is probably normal behaviour.

I clean the fluff filters after every load, and I did the bottom filter thing two weeks ago and it looked clean. The load is pretty full, it's the Cotton Cupboard Dry programme, and the washer spins at 1000. The clothes do come out fully dry in the end, it just takes ages. Is 3 and a half hours really normal then?

Yes, 3.5 hours is very likely normal for a heat-pump dryer, especially compared to your old condenser model. Here is why: A heat-pump dryer works like a fridge running in reverse. It dries clothes at a lower temperature (which feels 'barely warm') to save energy and be gentler on fabrics. Because the air isn't as hot, it takes longer to evaporate moisture. Your old condenser dryer used high heat, so it dried fast but was harsher on clothes and used more electricity. The fact that your towels are coming out fully dry at the end suggests the machine is working; it just needs more time. However, drying times can get even worse if airflow is restricted. You mentioned cleaning the bottom filter two weeks ago, but these condenser units often trap a fine layer of lint sludge inside the mesh that isn't obvious until you rinse it well. Even if it looked clean, a thorough rinse under a tap is worth doing to ensure maximum efficiency. Please try rinsing that condenser unit again and running a load. If the time doesn't improve significantly after that, let me know.
Ok I'll give the bottom filter another rinse and run a load. Anything else I should be checking while I'm at it? I do keep opening the door to see how it's getting on, if that matters.

Yes, opening the door does matter. Every time you open it during a cycle, you lose heat and moisture, which forces the machine to work harder and longer to get back on track. Try to resist checking it until the cycle is finished. The next biggest factor is airflow inside the drum. You mentioned the load is 'pretty full'. Heat pump dryers rely on air circulating freely around the clothes; if the drum is stuffed, the air can't reach the centre of the pile, which drastically extends drying times. Try running a smaller load (no more than two-thirds full) next time and see if that cuts the 3.5 hours down closer to the expected 2-3 hours. If reducing the load size makes a noticeable difference, then your machine is working exactly as it should—it just needs space to breathe.
Ok, I'll try not to keep opening the door, though it's hard! It's in my garage and it's pretty cold out there at the moment, about 8-10 degrees. Does that make any difference?

Yes, it does make a difference. Heat-pump dryers work by extracting heat from the air around them to warm up the drum. If the machine is in a garage at 8–10°C, there is less ambient heat for it to harvest, so the compressor has to work harder and longer to reach the drying temperature. This can easily add 30–60 minutes to your cycle time compared to running it in a warm utility room. Given that:
1. The clothes are coming out fully dry (just slowly).
2. It feels barely warm (which is how heat-pumps operate).
3. It is significantly slower than your old condenser model (which used high energy to blast hot air).
4. It is in a cold garage. Your dryer is probably working correctly. The combination of the machine's inherent efficiency and the low ambient temperature explains the 3.5-hour cycle time. If you can move it to a warmer room, you might see the times drop closer to 2–2.5 hours, but if not, this is just the reality of drying in a cold space with an efficient heat-pump machine.
